newsitem.title: UKRAINE: Foreigners say Ukraine T-bill limit unrealistic.
newsitem.headline: Foreigners say Ukraine T-bill limit unrealistic.

text.p: Ukraine's talk of limiting foreign investment in Treasury bills, which could reach hundreds of millions of dollars in the next few months, are unrealistic, bankers and economists said.
"They can't afford to throw foreigners out," said Juergen Conrad, an international economist at the German Advisory Group on Economic Reforms of Ukraine and at Deutsche Bank Research.
"Several hundreds of millions of dollars are ready to go into T-bills. It is happening now," Conrad told Reuters.
The relative stability of the new hryvnia currency and slowing inflation have made the market attractive to foreigners.

But a top central bank official said the Finance Ministry was gently telling non-residents it preferred Ukrainian investment, and had cut back on issue volumes at this week's auctions to discourage foreigners.
The official said non-resident buying accounted for up to 80 percent of T-bill market activity.

"Some Ukrainian specialists think they can afford to go without foreign buying," Conrad said. "They didn't meet their targets last year without foreigners. The same is true for 1997. It's crystal clear."

Yields for Ukrainian T-bills have fallen steadily in the past few months from over 100 percent last June. The National Bank of Ukraine (NBU) auctions the securities, usually twice weekly, on the ministry's behalf.
This week the yield on nine-month T-bills fell to 42.31 from 54.61 percent and to 47.01 from 56.90 percent on 12-month paper, helped by the cut in volumes.
Conrad forecast 42 percent yields on three-month bills and 48 percent yields on six-month bills in the next few months.

He said the government hopes to issue 2.5 trillion hryvnia ($1.3 trillion) worth of paper this year to finance the deficit -- whose final figure is not yet known because of delays in passing the 1997 budget -- after 1.5 trillion hryvnia in 1996.
Parliamentary approval for the tough budget draft would also clear the way for a $2.5 to $3 billion Extended Fund Facility (EFF) from the International Monetary Fund (IMF).
Conrad said local banks do not have the investment money foreign buyers do. He said Ukraine's Eurobond issue planned for this year would not cover the deficit.

Dealers said the largest foreign buyers of T-bills, which the ministry began issuing in March 1995 and opened to foreign buyers last autumn, were CS First Boston, Societe Generale, and Credit Lyonnais. Banks in Cyprus and the Baltic states, probably handling Russian money, are also big investors, they said.

Valeria Gontareva, Kiev's Societe Generale representative, declined to comment on how much her bank was spending on Ukrainian T-bills but said foreign buying was accounting for no less than 50 percent of market activity.
She said foreign limitation rules were only an idea, and yields and volumes were falling because the ministry does not yet know how much it needs to raise in 1997.
"If the budget was accepted the NBU would know the size of the budget deficit," she said. ($ = 1.879 Ukrainian Hryvnia)
